## Social Status and Mobility

### Objective and subjective social status

Research on the social foundations of distributive preferences has traditionally relied on objective indicators of position, such as income, education and occupational class, and on a self-interest logic according to which those who benefit least from redistribution support it least [@alesina_intergenerational_2018; @lindh_class_2020]. Because SSS only partly reflects these indicators [@tan_association_2020], the mismatch between them can be as informative as either level. Using the same panel data as this study, Bargain et al. [@bargain_social_2026] show that what predicts participation in the 2019 protests is not SSS itself but its gap with objective position: the further people place themselves below what their objective position would suggest, the more likely they are to protest.

Two caveats qualify the evidence linking SSS to distributive preferences. First, the subjective gradient depends on context: in more unequal countries, people with high SSS also support redistribution more, narrowing the gap between status groups [@melli_uncovering_2025]. Highly unequal and strongly commodified settings such as Chile may therefore be cases where SSS adds less than expected. Second, most of this evidence relies on differences between individuals. Panel studies suggest that redistributive preferences are fairly stable, anchored in long-term economic position and early socialisation, and shift mainly after large and often transitory shocks [@margalit_explaining_2013; @ogrady_how_2019], although fairness views do respond to individual events such as unemployment or promotion (Hvidberg et al., 2023). Whether the association between status and distributive preferences reflects stable between-person differences or within-person adjustment as status changes therefore remains open, and answering it requires separating the two sources of variation [@bell_explaining_2015].

### Past and expected mobility 

Status is not just a position, but also a trajectory: where people come from and where they hope to go can matter just as much as where they are. The literature on mobility has suggested that prospects for upward mobility can moderate demands for redistribution [@benabou_social_2001; @alesina_intergenerational_2018] and that, as with status, perceived mobility has greater attitudinal consequences than objective mobility [@gugushvili_intergenerational_2016; @hiltner_view_2024]. These effects, however, are not uniform. They vary depending on the type of policy or social service in question [@gugushvili_multilevel_2019], and when mobility is measured objectively, people tend to adopt the preferences of their destination position rather than those of their origin [@jaime-castillo_social_2019].

Expectations about the future, in particular, seem to carry more weight than past mobility [@schuck_how_2019], but the direction of their effect depends on how that upward mobility is expected to be achieved. If the next generation’s prospects are tied to public provision, optimism regarding one’s children may be accompanied by greater support for public services and less acceptance of the idea that access should depend on the ability to pay [@cojocaru_prospects_2014].

### Status, Mobility and Inequality Preferences

These debates have rarely been applied to market justice preferences—that is, to the idea that it is fair for access to services such as pensions, health care, and education to depend on the ability to pay. Comparative evidence suggests that these preferences are reinforced where private provision is most widespread [@lindh_public_2015; @immergut_it_2020], making Chile—with its widely commercialized pensions, health care, and education—a paradigmatic case. Previous studies using the same panel data have examined the role of perceived inequality [@castillo_perceptions_2025: @castillo_justification_2026], but the roles of objective and subjective status—and how they change over time—have not been addressed jointly. The question therefore remains open as to whether market justice preferences respond to the position people occupy, the one they believe they occupy, or the one they hope to attain—and whether they do so as stable differences between individuals or as changes within each individual. Answering this requires measuring subjective status in its past, present, and future dimensions (origin, self, and children) and separating these two sources of variation.
